docs.dcterms_abstract:
Thinks B. has made an unhappy choice for the subject of
his book, for learned women are ridiculed at the
present time. Has found Lady Pakington's Prayers
and will send B. a transcript. Wants to know what was
the MS. he saw at Queens College, and how it came there. [Bodleian card catalogue]


Apologises for not writing sooner, pleading poor health. Sympathises with his
disappointments and expresses cynicism as to the current lack of concern with
learning. Fears that education, especially in women, is undervalued. Inquires
whether he would care for Lady Packington’s prayers, which she has finally
found. [Dawn Hollis]

ox_transcription: Sarah Chapone catalogue Transcription by James Harrison (ed. Callum Seddon), February 2016. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 1 From Sarah Chapone to George Ballard 30 March 1753 Bodleian Library, Oxford MS Ballard 43, fols 188r –189v [fol. 188r] To1 Mr Ballard at Magdalen College Oxford Free Iii Gore [fol. 188v] [Blank] [fol. 189r] Sir,2 I received the five Books Yesterday very safe you had advertized me of; but find your putting up only that number, my Brother had mistaken me, as I had desired him to acquaint you that I beged eight Books which I would take care to receive the Receipts for, and convey to you Sir, excepting \those for/ my Brother’s and my own, which my Mama has at Cheltenham. The 1 Address written at a ninety -degree angle. 2 This letter was written on a single sheet of paper folded once to form a small, folio booklet, leaving four pages for the let ter itself. The first page is blank, and the second (foliated as 91, and then later, as 189), third, and fourth sides were used for the content of the letter. I follow the folio numbers used by the archivist at the Bodleian who foliated this manuscript, and record when the text runs to a ‘new’ page in footnotes. Sarah Chapone catalogue Transcription by James Harrison (ed. Callum Seddon), February 2016. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 2 Three Books still wanting, are for Mr Lewes, in Cork Street, Mr Dyer at Chelsea, and Dr M orley in Lincolns Inn Feilds; which I should be glad were sent immediately, as the Gentlemen are a little impatient for the Work since the Publication. I am sorry my Brother had it not in his Power to make his Visit longer at Oxford, as I know it would have given him Pleasure; he fell ill on the Road six miles short of Cheltenham, his Disorder [fol. 189v] proved the Mearzles which kept him some days at the Inn where my Mamas tender care soon enabled him to accompany her home; an d I had the great satisfaction of receiving a few lines from him on Wednesday. which assure me he is quite recovered. I believe Mr Richardson subscribed to your Work by my Brother’s hand, yet neither he nor I are quite sure as Mr Richardson can’t recollect whether it was to Mrs Delany, or my Brother. but when I write Cheltenham, I will enquire, and let you know, who is your debter. Mr Rickardson had no Receipt. he charges me with his Compliments. You were not so good to mention your own health, but which I hope you have enjoyed, without those sad Interruptions you have Sarah Chapone catalogue Transcription by James Harrison (ed. Callum Seddon), February 2016. Transcription hosted by EMLO. docs.dcterms_abstract:
Practical details about preparations for her voyage, e.g., bought
one doz. calico shifts at 8s. a piece, bought a mattress in a shop
in Fenchurch Street; has packed two chests as her things are all
to go away on Thursday next - a vast undertaking: I have taken an
account of what is put in every chest. I have a little parlour to
myself underground of which I keep the key. I have a fire there.
She has had a call from Miss Edgerton (to be her companion), a good
natured lady 10 years older than herself with whom she spoke of
cabin furniture. She hopes G. will excuse such a scrawl as I am so
hurried and surrounded with things and only a box to write upon.
She proceeds with charming details and expressions of gratitude.

docs.dcterms_abstract:
She comments with great general approval and appreciation on P's
book of seven sermons, singling out certain aspects. She sees
difficulty in the incarnation of the angelic being, is exceedingly
charmed with the sermon on the happiness of virtue: but does not
accept the belief that the goodness of God means that happiness
greatly preponderates in the world; she cannot reconcile this idea
with the miseries of life and in her opinion the goodness of God
does not rest upon it. "The miseries of life even if shown to be
greater than its enjoyments would not stagger my faith in the goodness
of God", "though He kill me yet will I trust in Him".

 [[It is a well-balanced and a good letter]
]   [[I am not certain I am
right in attributing it to Mrs. H. Chapone, who however is the only
person of that name in the D.N.B. There is no indication in the
letter that it is written by a woman But I hazard that she is the
writer]
]

I endeavour To hope Mr. Perry’s presence may have by this time prov’d the Most sovereign medicine, but I have much fear . in proportion 1 This letter is addressed to Charles Augustus West, a page to George III . He eloped with Charlotte Perry and they married secretly at Gretna Green. A year later t he marriage was formalized at St Luke’s Church in Chelsea [notes provided by the donor of the letters] . This letter is written in very neat handwriting and there is a larger space between this superscription at the top of the p age and the main body of the letter; presumably Penelope Maitland chose to write the letter in this way out of respect for a man who m she did not know very well. I am all impatience to hear of her, & of the effect of your letter To Mr. Perry: and tho’ I feel unreasonabl e in asking any moments of your time [page break ] so2 anxiously engag’d, I am yet persuaded your disposition is such as to readily admit my apology; and that you will favour me with accounts of my dr. Mrs. West ’till she is able to write. I have often experienc’d the Benefit of that very simple expedient Lemonade in a feverish Cold; may I hope she will try it, on my re= =commendation, in case there is no sympton to render it improper? my kindest Love attends her. I think myself much hon or’d, Sir, by the requ est with which You Conclude your letter, and beg leave to assure you I shal be Happy in every opportunity of proving to you that it is one Highly agreeable to Sir Your oblig’d & obed [ien]t H[onor a]ble Servant 2 The writing on the verso is perfectly spaced so that the same gap of around six lines is left at the top and the bottom of the page. Feb:ry for which I am inexpresibly oblig’d to you; That you should so punctually remember me at a time of Such Interesting concerns, demands my particular acknowledg= =ment. I unfeignedly Congratulate you and my dear charlotte On her (again) safe delivery, and the Birth of another fine Son. I am happy to hear her time was good , as Times go , but The account of her very delicate health distresses me much. the Advancing season I trust will be greatly beneficial to he r; and I will give up any satisfaction sooner than purchase it So dear as at the Expence of her health. when ever she is able To Write at all, I lay my commands upon her to confine her Pen to very short letters, cheifly accounts of her health &c ’till she Is stronger & may lengthen them with safety to herself. I will Write when in my power. and should have fulfill’d my pro= =mise in Writing again, had I not been Extreamly ill. I kept my room 6 Weeks with Excrutiating rheumatism Bodleian Student Editions Transcription by Charlotte Kinnear, Tilly Guthrie , and Leon Hughes; c hecked and edited by Mike Webb. Transcription hosted by EMLO. Please see citation guidelines at : emlo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about . 2 & other Complaints. and have never been out of the house since the 18 of December. the excessive severity of the Cold Or Dampness of the Weather throughout the Winter, has kept me from perfect recovery; & tho’ much better (I thank God) I am yet much oppress’d with A defluxion in m y head of An un [[com]]mon nature & to an uncommon degree. I will give [page break ] a more particular account of myself when I write to my dear Charlotte, as it would be an impertinent subject here, Mean time, I beg to assure her of my sincerest aff ections, and pray= =ers for her perfect recovery both from her present confinement and all her other ailments; And that the addition to her family May be the increase of her Happiness; in which wish, I Very heartily include yourself; whose Domestick Virtues I Have form’d the highest opinion of. I hope my lovely Freind will be careful to the utmost degree Of cold — in her getting up , changing her apartment & going out. I am happy to know she has a Nurse about her who has her Interest & yours so much at heart, as your own Mother, And you are an Excellent one as Deputy I dare say. So that With Others, she wants not care . My Love, Blessing & half a dozen Kisses to my sweet Godson — I Wish him joy of his little Playfellow.
